literature.lead_zh: 本期诺如病毒研究集中呈现以下进展。
key_findings_zh: RdRp区域和VP1区域的打字准确率分别达到97.6%和99.3%。对测试集中每个基因型的精确度、召回率和 F1 分数的分析表明,40 个 RdRp 基因型和 34 个 VP1 基因型的所有指标均≥ 0.9。所有长度间隔的打字准确度≥ 0.96。 [10.1007/s00705-026-06777-0]
用诺如病毒 GII.4 VP1 mRNA或脂质纳米颗粒配制的VP1 mRNA转染诱导细胞内和细胞外VP1表达。蔗糖梯度纯化和电子显微镜证实了VLP组装。这些颗粒保留了关键的抗原和功能特性,包括被人血清中的 诺如病毒 特异性抗体识别以及与组织血型抗原的结合。 [10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129272]
总体而言,118 个样本中有 61 个(51.7%)检测出至少一种病毒呈阳性。与地下水(15.4%;8/52 个样本)相比,地表水(河流)的污染率(80.3%;53/66 个样本)要高得多。 [10.1007/s12560-026-09712-3]
本文探讨了围绕 诺如病毒 暴发 不断变化的证据,考虑了自 COVID-19 大流行以来吸取的经验教训,并根据当前英国指南和感染预防标准讨论了对社区护理实践的实际影响。 [10.12968/bjcn.2026.0137]
2b 期试验的血清证明,传统 96 孔和小型 384 孔测定格式之间的 nAb 反应高度一致 (r=0.95),并且 nAb 和 HBGA 阻断抗体之间的强相关性使得能够进行血清保护的 诺如病毒 免疫分析。 [10.1016/j.jviromet.2026.115482]

papers.title: Construction of a machine learning model for dual-region typing of norovirus RdRp and VP1 based on genomic k-mer features
papers.abstract: Norovirus (NoV), a major global acute gastroenteritis pathogen, has high genetic diversity. Developing precise, rapid typing methods is crucial for epidemic control and vaccine development. Thus, this study develops a machine learning tool based on Norovirus genomic k-mer (length-k nucleotide fragments) features. It enables rapid, accurate dual-region typing of RdRp (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) and VP1 (major capsid protein) without alignment or segmentation. Using k-mer frequency features with k = 11, the MurmurHash3 algorithm maps the features to a 220-dimensional space and constructs a hash feature table. A random forest model comprising 500 decision trees is then used. Each tree randomly selects 20 features during node splitting. The model is trained and evaluated using a bootstrap sampling strategy (80% training and 20% out-of-bag estimation), and prediction confidence intervals are outputted. The typing accuracy rates for the RdRp region and VP1 region reached 97.6% and 99.3%, respectively. Analysis of precision, recall, and F1-score for each genotype in the test set showed that all metrics for the 40 RdRp genotypes and 34 VP1 genotypes were ≥ 0.9. Typing accuracy across all length intervals was ≥ 0.96. This study integrates machine learning and bioinformatics to develop a novel norovirus genome analysis tool. It enables precise genotyping despite multi-region interference and reveals hidden genomic information, supporting viral classification and tracing. The feature hashing and ensemble learning strategies overcome traditional dependencies on alignment and annotation, offering a universal, efficient, scalable framework for viral genome identification.

papers.source_body_en: Norovirus (NoV), a major global acute gastroenteritis pathogen, has high genetic diversity. Developing precise, rapid typing methods is crucial for epidemic control and vaccine development. Thus, this study develops a machine learning tool based on Norovirus genomic k-mer (length-k nucleotide fragments) features. It enables rapid, accurate dual-region typing of RdRp (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) and VP1 (major capsid protein) without alignment or segmentation. Using k-mer frequency features with k = 11, the MurmurHash3 algorithm maps the features to a 220-dimensional space and constructs a hash feature table. A random forest model comprising 500 decision trees is then used. Each tree randomly selects 20 features during node splitting. The model is trained and evaluated using a bootstrap sampling strategy (80% training and 20% out-of-bag estimation), and prediction confidence intervals are outputted. The typing accuracy rates for the RdRp region and VP1 region reached 97.6% and 99.3%, respectively. Analysis of precision, recall, and F1-score for each genotype in the test set showed that all metrics for the 40 RdRp genotypes and 34 VP1 genotypes were ≥ 0.9. Typing accuracy across all length intervals was ≥ 0.96. This study integrates machine learning and bioinformatics to develop a novel norovirus genome analysis tool. It enables precise genotyping despite multi-region interference and reveals hidden genomic information, supporting viral classification and tracing. The feature hashing and ensemble learning strategies overcome traditional dependencies on alignment and annotation, offering a universal, efficient, scalable framework for viral genome identification.

papers.title: mRNA encoding norovirus VP1 produces antigenically functional virus-like particles in vitro
papers.abstract: Human norovirus is a leading cause of acute gastroenteritis worldwide across all age groups, yet no licensed vaccine is available. The major capsid protein, VP1, self-assembles into highly immunogenic virus-like particles (VLPs) that have shown promise in clinical studies. Recently, mRNA has emerged as a compelling platform for norovirus vaccination. However, whether VP1-encoding mRNA can drive authentic VLP formation in human cells relevant to the vaccination environment has remained unknown. In this study, we used multiple human cell lines, including THP-1-derived macrophage-like cells, to model the post-vaccination environment. Transfection with norovirus GII.4 VP1 mRNA or lipid nanoparticle-formulated VP1 mRNA induced both intracellular and extracellular VP1 expression. Sucrose gradient purification and electron microscopy confirmed VLP assembly. These particles retained key antigenic and functional properties, including recognition by norovirus-specific antibodies in human serum and binding to histo-blood group antigens. Collectively, our findings provide direct evidence that VP1-encoding mRNA can generate structurally and functionally relevant norovirus VLPs in physiologically relevant human cell systems. These results strengthen the mechanistic rationale for mRNA-based norovirus vaccines and support their continued development.

papers.title: Occurrence and distribution of Sapovirus in shellfish.
papers.abstract: Shellfish harbour emerging enteric viruses including sapovirus that are often not the main target for routine shellfish safety screening. Thus, the present investigation aimed at assessing the occurrence of sapovirus in 2450 shellfish samples using standard procedures and random-intercept logistic-regression modelling. The overall prevalence of shellfish-borne sapovirus was 17.14% (95% CI: 8.95-30.34). Sapovirus prevalence in shellfish was significantly different (p ≤ 0.0005) by shellfish type, family, genus, species, RNA extraction, nation and continent. Cockles (Cardiidae) showed the highest pooled sapovirus prevalence (∼26%), followed by clams (∼13%) and oysters (∼11). Among species, Perna spp had high-pooled sapovirus rate (66.5%), while Crassostrea gigas had 14%. papers.abstract_zh: 贝类含有新出现的肠道病毒,包括沙波病毒,这些病毒通常不是常规贝类安全筛查的主要目标。因此,本研究旨在使用标准程序和随机截取逻辑回归模型评估 2450 个贝类样本中沙波病毒的发生情况。贝类沙波病毒的总体 患病率 为 17.14% (95% CI: 8.95-30.34)。贝类中的沙波病毒 患病率 因贝类类型、科、属、种、RNA 提取、国家和大陆的不同而存在显着差异 (p ≤ 0.0005)。鸟蛤(Cardiidae)显示出最高的混合沙波病毒 患病率 (∼26%),其次是蛤 (∼13%) 和牡蛎 (∼11)。在物种中,珍珠贝的混合沙波病毒率较高(66.5%),而巨牡蛎为14%。此外,贝类中沙波病毒 患病率 最高的国家是西班牙(35.8%)、巴西(25.3%)、意大利(18.2%)和日本(17.2%)。按大陆划分,南美洲(25.3%)和欧洲(14.3%),贝类中沙波病毒的总比率超过亚洲(10.31%)和非洲(11.6%)。该研究确定检测方法和 RNA 提取试剂盒(作为重要调节剂)会影响贝类中检测和准确确定沙波病毒 患病率 (p≈0.05) 的能力。在测试的 9 个因素中,国家和检测分析显着调节了贝类中的沙波病毒 患病率。值得注意的是,贝类物种、属、国家、试剂盒、大陆、科、检测分析、贝类类型、病毒质量控制、年份和样本量解释了 67.27%、56.93%、55.48%、43.51%、38.92%、35.89%、28.14%、23.36%、18.06%、4.74% 和贝类中沙波病毒混合 患病率 的真实方差分别为 1.81%。总之,这项研究表明贝类的沙波病毒污染很常见。贝类中混合的沙波病毒 患病率 在某些双壳类和场所中的比率特别高,这表明沙波病毒与 诺如病毒 一样是贝类安全问题。研究结果强调了将沙波病毒纳入常规贝类监测和贝类相关 暴发 调查的重要性,以补充 诺如病毒 监测。

papers.title: Optimization and Miniaturization of a Human Intestinal Organoid Neutralization Assay for Evaluating Human Norovirus Antibody Responses.
papers.abstract: Human noroviruses (HuNoVs) are the principal etiological agents of acute viral gastroenteritis worldwide. While conventional 96-well human intestinal organoid (HIO) neutralization assays provide a physiologically relevant assessment of neutralizing antibody (nAb) responses, sample volume requirements (50μL for 96 wells vs. 12.5μL serum for 384 wells per titration) and 96-well plate capacity limit the application for large-scale clinical and vaccine studies. Here, we describe the development of a miniaturized 384-well HIO neutralization assay for nAb responses to HuNoV. Sera from a phase 2b trial of a bivalent GI.1 and consensus GII.4 virus-like particle norovirus vaccine candidate demonstrated high concordance in nAb responses to the predominant GII.4 Sydney variant between conventional 96-well and miniaturized 384-well assay formats (r= 0.95). Further, a strong correlation between nAb and histo-blood group antigen (HBGA)-blocking antibodies enables serum-sparing (25μL per titration, 4-fold reduction) norovirus immune profiling, supporting scalable deployment in large clinical trials. The 384-well plate neutralization assay maintains assay sensitivity, and concordance with the 96-well format increases scalability by allowing more samples per plate and reducing serum requirements.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to optimize and miniaturize a human intestinal organoid neutralization assay for evaluating human norovirus antibody responses, addressing the need for a scalable method for large-scale clinical and vaccine studies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved developing a miniaturized 384-well human intestinal organoid neutralization assay for nAb responses to HuNoV, using sera from a phase 2b trial of a bivalent GI.1 and GII.4 virus-like particle norovirus vaccine candidate.
analysis.methods: The miniaturized 384-well HIO neutralization assay was developed, maintaining assay sensitivity and concordance with the 96-well format, allowing more samples per plate and reducing serum requirements.
analysis.main_results: Sera from a phase 2b trial demonstrated high concordance in nAb responses between conventional 96-well and miniaturized 384-well assay formats (r=0.95), and a strong correlation between nAb and HBGA-blocking antibodies enabled serum-sparing norovirus immune profiling.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The miniaturized assay supports scalable deployment in large clinical trials, providing a physiologically relevant assessment of neutralizing antibody responses to HuNoV.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The miniaturized assay can inform surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment of norovirus gastroenteritis by enabling more efficient and scalable immune profiling.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the need for further validation in different populations and the potential for assay sensitivity reduction with miniaturization, but the evidence suggests moderate confidence in the assay's performance.

analysis.summary_en: This study optimized and miniaturized a human intestinal organoid neutralization assay for evaluating human norovirus antibody responses, demonstrating high concordance with the conventional 96-well format and enabling serum-sparing norovirus immune profiling, supporting scalable deployment in large clinical trials.

papers.title_zh: 用于评估人类 诺如病毒 抗体反应的人类肠道类器官中和测定的优化和小型化。
papers.source_body_en: Human noroviruses (HuNoVs) are the principal etiological agents of acute viral gastroenteritis worldwide. While conventional 96-well human intestinal organoid (HIO) neutralization assays provide a physiologically relevant assessment of neutralizing antibody (nAb) responses, sample volume requirements (50μL for 96 wells vs. 12.5μL serum for 384 wells per titration) and 96-well plate capacity limit the application for large-scale clinical and vaccine studies. Here, we describe the development of a miniaturized 384-well HIO neutralization assay for nAb responses to HuNoV. Sera from a phase 2b trial of a bivalent GI.1 and consensus GII.4 virus-like particle norovirus vaccine candidate demonstrated high concordance in nAb responses to the predominant GII.4 Sydney variant between conventional 96-well and miniaturized 384-well assay formats (r= 0.95). Further, a strong correlation between nAb and histo-blood group antigen (HBGA)-blocking antibodies enables serum-sparing (25μL per titration, 4-fold reduction) norovirus immune profiling, supporting scalable deployment in large clinical trials. The 384-well plate neutralization assay maintains assay sensitivity, and concordance with the 96-well format increases scalability by allowing more samples per plate and reducing serum requirements.

papers.title: Multi-Virus Surveillance Across Diverse Freshwater Systems in Tehran, Iran.
papers.abstract: Environmental surveillance of viral contaminants in water systems is an essential tool for assessing exposure risk and supporting early-warning frameworks for emerging infectious diseases. In this study, a comprehensive one-year surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 and six enteric viruses was conducted across diverse freshwater systems in Tehran, Iran - including rivers, wells, and traditional qanat (underground aqueduct) infrastructures. Water quality parameters (turbidity, pH, Total Dissolved Solids, nitrate) and fecal bacterial indicators (total coliforms, fecal coliforms, and E. coli) were also measured to contextualize viral contamination within a broader environmental risk framework. Between September 2020 and August 2021, a total of 118 water samples were collected and analyzed using quantitative molecular detection methods. Overall, 61 of 118 samples (51.7%) tested positive for at least one virus. Surface water (rivers) showed substantially higher contamination rates (80.3%; 53/66 samples) compared to groundwater (15.4%; 8/52 samples). Among groundwater sources, qanat systems were markedly more vulnerable than conventional wells, with 25.0% (6/24) of qanat samples testing positive versus only 7.1% (2/28) of well samples. This elevated contamination in qanats was dominated by rotavirus (5/6 positive qanat samples, detection rate 20.8%) and was associated with higher fecal bacterial loads (total coliform geometric mean: 245 MPN/100 mL in qanats vs. 28 MPN/100 mL in wells), consistent with the susceptibility of shallow horizontal collection channels to fecal infiltration. SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in 34.8% of river samples and 3.9% of groundwater samples, with concentrations reaching 1.28 × 104 genome copies per liter (GC/L) in surface waters, demonstrating sustained fecal contamination across all seasons. The most prevalent viruses in river water were norovirus GII (45.5%), adenovirus (43.9%), rotavirus (42.4%), and norovirus GI (40.9%), with mean concentrations ranging from 1.26 × 102 to 3.76 × 103 GC/L. Hepatitis A and E viruses were not detected in any sample. Seasonal variation in viral detection was observed for enteric viruses, while SARS-CoV-2 and adenovirus showed year-round persistence. Strong correlations between fecal indicators and viral contamination (Spearman r = 0.61-0.63) support the use of bacterial monitoring as a cost-effective screening proxy. The results highlight the particular vulnerability of qanat systems and underscore the value of integrated environmental surveillance for water safety management in arid, water-stressed urban environments.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 水系统中病毒污染物的环境 监测 是评估暴露风险和支持新发传染病预警框架的重要工具。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 在这项研究中,对伊朗德黑兰的不同淡水系统(包括河流、水井和传统坎儿井(地下渡槽)基础设施)进行了为期一年的 SARS-CoV-2 和六种肠道病毒综合 监测 调查。
elements_zh.methods: 2020年9月至2021年8月期间,共采集118份水样,并采用定量分子检测方法进行分析。
elements_zh.main_results: 总体而言,118 个样本中有 61 个(51.7%)检测出至少一种病毒呈阳性。与地下水(15.4%;8/52 个样本)相比,地表水(河流)的污染率(80.3%;53/66 个样本)要高得多。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 河水中最常见的病毒是诺如病毒 GII (45.5%)、腺病毒(43.9%)、轮状病毒(42.4%)和诺如病毒 GI (40.9%),平均浓度范围为1.26 × 102至3.76 × 103 GC/L。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 粪便指标和病毒污染之间的强相关性(Spearman r = 0.61-0.63)支持使用细菌监测作为具有成本效益的筛查代理。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 肠道病毒的病毒检测存在季节性变化,而 SARS-CoV-2 和腺病毒则全年持续存在。

Surface water (rivers) showed substantially higher contamination rates (80.3%; 53/66 samples) compared to groundwater (15.4%; 8/52 samples). This elevated contamination in qanats was dominated by rotavirus (5/6 positive qanat samples, detection rate 20.8%) and was associated with higher fecal bacterial loads (total coliform geometric mean: 245 MPN/100 mL in qanats vs. 28 MPN/100 mL in wells), consistent with the susceptibility of shallow horizontal collection channels to fecal infiltration. SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in 34.8% of river samples and 3.9% of groundwater samples, with concentrations reaching 1.28 × 104 genome copies per liter (GC/L) in surface waters, demonstrating sustained fecal contamination across all seasons. The most prevalent viruses in river water were norovirus GII (45.5%), adenovirus (43.9%), rotavirus (42.4%), and norovirus GI (40.9%), with mean concentrations ranging from 1.26 × 102 to 3.76 × 103 GC/L. Hepatitis A and E viruses were not detected in any sample. Seasonal variation in viral detection was observed for enteric viruses, while SARS-CoV-2 and adenovirus showed year-round persistence. Strong correlations between fecal indicators and viral contamination (Spearman r = 0.61-0.63) support the use of bacterial monitoring as a cost-effective screening proxy. The results highlight the particular vulnerability of qanat systems and underscore the value of integrated environmental surveillance for water safety management in arid, water-stressed urban environments.

papers.title: Etiology and incidence of diarrhea requiring hospitalization in children under 5 years of age in 31 low- and middle-income countries: Findings from the Global Pediatric Diarrhea Surveillance network, 2017-2022.
papers.abstract: Diarrhea remains a leading cause of child morbidity and mortality. Improved and ongoing estimates of the etiology of hospitalized pediatric diarrhea in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are needed to help prioritize and evaluate the use of existing and upcoming vaccines and interventions. The Global Pediatric Diarrhea Surveillance (GPDS) network is a World Health Organization (WHO)-coordinated public health surveillance network investigating the etiology of hospitalized diarrhea among children aged <5 years in LMICs. The GPDS network enrolls children hospitalized with diarrhea at 38 sentinel surveillance sites in 31 LMICs. Randomly selected stool specimens were tested by TaqMan Array Card quantitative reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) for 16 pathogens associated with diarrhea. We estimated pathogen-specific attributable fractions (AFs) and incidence of diarrheal hospitalizations at the global, regional, and country levels during 3 time periods: 2017-2018, 2019-2020, and 2021-2022, with a focus on the most recent results. During 2017-2022, the GPDS network enrolled 70,750 children aged <5 years hospitalized with diarrhea, of which 16,458 (23.3%) were randomly selected for qPCR testing. The most prevalent pathogen detected, regardless of quantity or modeled etiologic attribution, was rotavirus (weighted prevalence 30.4%), followed by adenovirus 40/41 (19.1%), norovirus (17.9%), Shigella (14.1%), and Campylobacter jejuni/coli (8.6%). Overall, in 2017-2022, rotavirus was the leading etiology globally (AF 32.5%; 95% Confidence Interval (CI): 27.4, 37.6), followed by Shigella (9.8%; 8.4, 11.3), adenovirus 40/41 (8.6%; 6.3, 10.8) and norovirus (6.7%; 5.6, 7.7). Over time, rotavirus consistently declined from an AF of 36.7% (95% CI: 28.7, 46.7) in 2017-2018 to 26.7% (20.7, 34.1) in 2021-2022. Norovirus AF increased slightly from 6.2% (4.7, 7.7) in 2017-2018 to 7.3% (5.0, 9.2) in 2021-2022. Global Shigella burden remained stable, and adenovirus 40/41 demonstrated significant volatility, peaking globally in 2019-2020 (11.9%; 5.9, 17.5). In 2021-2022, rotavirus was the leading cause of hospitalized diarrhea in 6 of 9 geographic groupings, norovirus predominated in Central and South America, and Shigella was the leading etiology in South Asia. In the subset of countries that had introduced rotavirus vaccine, the leading etiologies in 2021-2022 were rotavirus (18.4%; 15.8, 21.5) and Shigella (16.4%; 11.8, 21.1). In 2021-2022, rotavirus had the highest attributable incidence of hospitalized diarrhea in children (2.3 per 1,000 child-years; 1.8, 3.0), followed by Shigella (0.9; 0.7, 1.1), norovirus (0.6; 0.4, 0.8) and adenovirus 40/41 (0.6; 0.4, 0.8). Despite the widespread use of rotavirus vaccines, rotavirus remained the leading cause of severe diarrhea among children aged <5 years in LMICs globally. However, the proportion of pediatric diarrhea attributable to rotavirus consistently declined from 2017-2018-2021-2022, and there were notable differences in the distribution of diarrheal etiologies between regions and across time periods. Shigella, norovirus, and enteric adenoviruses were also associated with a substantial burden of disease. Improving the efficacy and coverage of rotavirus vaccination and prioritizing interventions against other enteric pathogens could further reduce diarrhea morbidity and mortality.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the etiology of hospitalized diarrhea in children under 5 years in 31 low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) from 2017 to 2022. It highlights that norovirus was the third most prevalent pathogen, with an attributable fraction (AF) of 6.7% (5.6, 7.7) globally. papers.title_zh: 31 个低收入和中等收入国家 5 岁以下儿童需要住院治疗的腹泻的病因和 发病率:来自全球小儿腹泻 发病率 网络的调查结果,2017-2022 年。
papers.source_body_en: Diarrhea remains a leading cause of child morbidity and mortality. Improved and ongoing estimates of the etiology of hospitalized pediatric diarrhea in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are needed to help prioritize and evaluate the use of existing and upcoming vaccines and interventions. The Global Pediatric Diarrhea Surveillance (GPDS) network is a World Health Organization (WHO)-coordinated public health surveillance network investigating the etiology of hospitalized diarrhea among children aged <5 years in LMICs. The GPDS network enrolls children hospitalized with diarrhea at 38 sentinel surveillance sites in 31 LMICs. Randomly selected stool specimens were tested by TaqMan Array Card quantitative reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) for 16 pathogens associated with diarrhea. We estimated pathogen-specific attributable fractions (AFs) and incidence of diarrheal hospitalizations at the global, regional, and country levels during 3 time periods: 2017-2018, 2019-2020, and 2021-2022, with a focus on the most recent results. During 2017-2022, the GPDS network enrolled 70,750 children aged <5 years hospitalized with diarrhea, of which 16,458 (23.3%) were randomly selected for qPCR testing. The most prevalent pathogen detected, regardless of quantity or modeled etiologic attribution, was rotavirus (weighted prevalence 30.4%), followed by adenovirus 40/41 (19.1%), norovirus (17.9%), Shigella (14.1%), and Campylobacter jejuni/coli (8.6%). Overall, in 2017-2022, rotavirus was the leading etiology globally (AF 32.5%; 95% Confidence Interval (CI): 27.4, 37.6), followed by Shigella (9.8%; 8.4, 11.3), adenovirus 40/41 (8.6%; 6.3, 10.8) and norovirus (6.7%; 5.6, 7.7). Over time, rotavirus consistently declined from an AF of 36.7% (95% CI: 28.7, 46.7) in 2017-2018 to 26.7% (20.7, 34.1) in 2021-2022. Norovirus AF increased slightly from 6.2% (4.7, 7.7) in 2017-2018 to 7.3% (5.0, 9.2) in 2021-2022. Global Shigella burden remained stable, and adenovirus 40/41 demonstrated significant volatility, peaking globally in 2019-2020 (11.9%; 5.9, 17.5). In 2021-2022, rotavirus was the leading cause of hospitalized diarrhea in 6 of 9 geographic groupings, norovirus predominated in Central and South America, and Shigella was the leading etiology in South Asia. In the subset of countries that had introduced rotavirus vaccine, the leading etiologies in 2021-2022 were rotavirus (18.4%; 15.8, 21.5) and Shigella (16.4%; 11.8, 21.1). In 2021-2022, rotavirus had the highest attributable incidence of hospitalized diarrhea in children (2.3 per 1,000 child-years; 1.8, 3.0), followed by Shigella (0.9; 0.7, 1.1), norovirus (0.6; 0.4, 0.8) and adenovirus 40/41 (0.6; 0.4, 0.8). Despite the widespread use of rotavirus vaccines, rotavirus remained the leading cause of severe diarrhea among children aged <5 years in LMICs globally. However, the proportion of pediatric diarrhea attributable to rotavirus consistently declined from 2017-2018-2021-2022, and there were notable differences in the distribution of diarrheal etiologies between regions and across time periods. Shigella, norovirus, and enteric adenoviruses were also associated with a substantial burden of disease. Improving the efficacy and coverage of rotavirus vaccination and prioritizing interventions against other enteric pathogens could further reduce diarrhea morbidity and mortality.

papers.title: A Narrative Review of the Norovirus Burden in Closed and Semi-Closed Structural Settings
papers.abstract: Noroviruses pose a major public health challenge in structurally closed or semi-closed settings where person-to-person contact, shared environment, and high-risk populations facilitate rapid transmission. This narrative review synthesizes epidemiological evidence on the burden of norovirus infection in closed and semi-closed settings, such as long-term care facilities (LTCFs), healthcare facilities, schools, childcare centers, and cruise ships, where norovirus transmission risk is elevated. Priority populations frequently experiencing high attack rates and patterns of key factors related to norovirus transmission are summarized for each context. Reported attack rates varied substantially both within and across settings, with elevated attack rates reported in LTCFs, healthcare facilities, childcare settings, and several other closed or semi-closed settings. Norovirus outbreaks are frequent and severe in closed and semi-closed settings, highlighting the need for targeted prevention and control measures in these contexts.

papers.full_text: AbstractIntroductionHuman parechovirus is a common pathogen causing respiratory and gastroenterological symptoms. Symptoms range from asymptomatic courses to rare encephalitis or sepsis-like symptoms. Studies regarding neurodevelopment after parechovirus encephalitis in infants are conflicting with indications of possible short or long term neurodevelopmental impairments. In this case report we describe an especially severe course of human parechovirus infection.CaseA two-week-old infant presented with fever and developed seizures and apneic episodes after admission. Laboratory tests revealed leukopenia. A lumbar puncture revealed parechovirus via polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Recurrent seizures required extensive anticonvulsive therapy. Invasive ventilation for four days was necessary due to apneic episodes. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed white matter involvement.DiscussionIn neonates with a sepsis-like presentation and largely unremarkable laboratory and cerebrospinal fluid findings, parechovirus encephalitis is an important differential diagnosis. In this case, follow-up examinations showed age-appropriate neurodevelopment. However, owing to the severe clinical presentation and extensive neuroimaging abnormalities, long-term neurodevelopmental monitoring is warranted.Keywords: case report, encephalitis, neonatal, parechovirus, seizures Timeline during the inpatient staySee Figure 1.Figure 1Timeline of the clinical course during the inpatient stay [aEEG-(amplitude-integrated) electroencephalography; MRI: magnetic resonance imaging; CSF- cerebrospinal fluid; EEG- electroencephalogram; IVIG- intravenous immunoglobulin; PICU- paediatric intensive care unit].Clinical timeline graphic showing three main sections: clinical presentation, diagnostics, and interventions. Key events include initial fever and ward admission, recurrent apnea and seizure escalation leading to PICU admission, then transfer and discharge. Diagnostics detail leukopenia, positive Parechovirus PCR, MRI changes, echocardiography, and EEG findings. Interventions include intubation, high-flow oxygen, anticonvulsants, IVIG, invasive ventilation on days two to five, and extubation. \n\nLet me know if you need alt text for a different image or require further details. If you have another image, please upload it or provide its URL.Diagnostic assessment, therapy and follow-upLaboratory findingsLaboratory investigations revealed leukopenia with lymphopenia and a mildly elevated interleukin-6 (IL-6) concentration. Mild hypernatremia and a slight elevation in serum bilirubin were also noted. The remaining serum electrolytes, liver and renal function parameters were within the reference ranges (Table 1).Table 1Pathological laboratory findings.ParameterNormResultLeukocytes7,8–15,91 10E9/L4,19 10E9/LNeutrophiles14–55%45%Lymphocytes34–77%30%Monocytes4–18%23%Eosinophiles<5%1%Basophiles<1%0%IL-6<7 ng/L84 ng/LNatrium136–145 mmol/L152 mmol/LBilirubin<1,2 mg/dL4,5 mg/dLStool PCR testing was negative for adenovirus, astrovirus, norovirus, sapovirus, and rotavirus.Metabolic test for vitamin B6 dependent epilepsy was negative.CSF findingsBecause of the recurrent seizures, a lumbar puncture was performed. Routine CSF analysis was unremarkable, with a leukocyte count of 1 cell/μL (reference range, 0–5 cells/μL). Multiplex PCR analysis of the CSF was positive for human parechovirus.ImagingInitial cranial ultrasonography was unremarkable. Brain MRI subsequently demonstrated extensive, bilateral symmetrical diffusion restriction involving the thalami, corpus callosum, and internal and external capsules (Figure 2). This pattern was consistent with severe human parechovirus encephalitis.Figure 2Brain magnetic resonance imaging during the acute phase and at three-month follow-up. (A) Initial diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (02/2025) demonstrating extensive bilateral and symmetrical diffusion abnormalities involving the thalami, corpus callosum, and internal and external capsules (red arrows). (B) Follow-up magnetic resonance imaging three months after discharge showing reduced supratentorial volume, predominantly affecting the white matter, and poor delineation of the corpus callosum. The previously observed diffusion abnormalities had resolved.Panel A shows a brain MRI scan with red arrows indicating areas of abnormal signal intensity in the deep white matter. Panel B presents a similar brain MRI scan without arrows, used for comparative assessment.Echocardiography showed normal cardiac morphology, dimensions and function.EEGOn the day of admission, amplitude-integrated electroencephalography (aEEG) demonstrated recurrent seizures with varying localisation, some of which were accompanied by clinical manifestations. The background activity was characterised by a persistent burst-suppression pattern.Treatment and courseAfter the onset of seizures, anticonvulsive treatment was initially commenced with pyridoxine (a single dose of 25 mg/kg) and phenobarbital. Because of persistent seizures, levetiracetam was subsequently added; however, adequate seizure control was only achieved with substantial delay. After the positive HPeV PCR result became available, pyridoxine was discontinued.The intravenous phenobarbital dose was increased to 8 mg/kg once daily. Levetiracetam was initiated at a dosage of 20 mg/kg intravenously twice daily.Empirical antimicrobial treatment for suspected meningitis/encephalitis was initiated with ceftriaxone (100 mg/kg once) and aciclovir (20 mg/kg once). Both agents were discontinued after the CSF results became available.Despite high-flow nasal oxygen therapy, recurrent apneic episodes requiring bag-mask ventilation occurred. The patient was therefore intubated on the first day of admission to the PICU. Invasive mechanical ventilation was continued for four days, and the patient was extubated following improvement of the aEEG findings. No further clinical seizures occurred during the hospital stay.During mechanical ventilation, the patient received a single intravenous dose of immunoglobulin (IVIG) at 1.5 g/kg because of the severity of the clinical presentation.After extubation, phenobarbital was continued at 4 mg/kg orally once daily and levetiracetam was continued orally at 30 mg/ kg twice daily.After discharge from the PICU, the patient subsequently remained on the general paediatric ward for six days. EEG demonstrated independent multifocal epileptiform sharp waves at both frontal regions, with right-sided predominance and activation during sleep.The patient was discharged on maintenance anticonvulsive therapy with phenobarbital and levetiracetam and received outpatient physiotherapy. At follow-up one month after discharge, EEG continued to demonstrate sharp waves.A further assessment three months after discharge, including brain MRI, revealed reduced supratentorial volume, predominantly affecting the white matter, and poor delineation of the corpus callosum (Figure 2). The previously observed white-matter diffusion restriction had resolved. Clinically, there was no evidence of relevant developmental delay.At the three-month follow-up, the patient had remained seizure-free for 11 weeks and the EEG was age-appropriate. Anticonvulsive medication was therefore discontinued. Another assessment at six months after discharge showed age-appropriate development of the patient and a normal EEG. Further follow-up assessment is scheduled for the age of 18 months to monitor his neurocognitive and developmental outcome. Clinical findingsOn admission, the infant was in an age-appropriate nutritional state but appeared generally unwell. His skin was pale pink, with mottling of the limbs. The anterior fontanelle was soft and flat. Heart sounds were normal and regular. Respiratory, abdominal, and ear, nose, and throat examinations were unremarkable.On neurological examination, the infant was somnolent but arousable and exhibited a high-pitched cry. Spontaneous movements, muscle tone, and strength were symmetrical.Because of the fever, the patient was initially admitted to the general paediatric ward for clinical observation. During the first hours of his inpatient stay, he developed recurrent apnoeas and seizures and was therefore transferred to the PICU.Following transfer to the PICU, the recurrent seizures were characterised more precisely as predominantly unilateral twitching of the upper limbs, occasionally accompanied by lip smacking. Individual episodes lasted 10–30 s and were associated with apnea and oxygen desaturation.During hospital stay, the infant developed a generalised erythematous rash. Laboratory findingsLaboratory investigations revealed leukopenia with lymphopenia and a mildly elevated interleukin-6 (IL-6) concentration. Mild hypernatremia and a slight elevation in serum bilirubin were also noted. The remaining serum electrolytes, liver and renal function parameters were within the reference ranges (Table 1).Table 1Pathological laboratory findings.ParameterNormResultLeukocytes7,8–15,91 10E9/L4,19 10E9/LNeutrophiles14–55%45%Lymphocytes34–77%30%Monocytes4–18%23%Eosinophiles<5%1%Basophiles<1%0%IL-6<7 ng/L84 ng/LNatrium136–145 mmol/L152 mmol/LBilirubin<1,2 mg/dL4,5 mg/dLStool PCR testing was negative for adenovirus, astrovirus, norovirus, sapovirus, and rotavirus.Metabolic test for vitamin B6 dependent epilepsy was negative. CSF findingsBecause of the recurrent seizures, a lumbar puncture was performed. Routine CSF analysis was unremarkable, with a leukocyte count of 1 cell/μL (reference range, 0–5 cells/μL). Multiplex PCR analysis of the CSF was positive for human parechovirus. DiscussionThis case illustrates an exceptionally severe course of neonatal human parechovirus infection. However, the findings are inherently limited by the single-patient nature of a case report. Moreover, the follow-up period of only six months precludes conclusions regarding the patient's long-term neurological and developmental outcome.HPeV is transmitted via the faecal–oral and respiratory routes, particularly through close contact within households (7). In the present case, several close family members had symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection, suggesting possible household transmission. However, as the family members were not tested for HPeV, the source and route of transmission could not be definitively established.The patient exhibited manifestations resembling those reported in other severe cases of HPeV infection. HPeV infections can cause a broad spectrum of symptoms depending on the viral genotype, ranging from fever and gastrointestinal or respiratory symptoms to sepsis-like illness, (meningo-) encephalitis, seizures, apnea, rash, myocarditis, hepatitis, and lethargy. Severe manifestations have been attributed, at least in part, to a systemic hyperinflammatory immune response. Viraemia may occur more frequently in young infants because of low levels of maternally derived antibodies and immaturity of the neonatal immune system. In addition, the greater permeability of the blood–brain barrier in young infants may facilitate viral neuroinvasion (7, 9, 10).Enteroviruses belong to the same viral family as HPeV and may cause a similar spectrum of disease, including fever, respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms, sepsis-like illness, (meningo-) encephalitis, hand, foot and mouth disease, herpangina, rash, myocarditis and hepatitis (11).Especially the generalized erythematous rash which our patient exhibited is a typical sign of HPeV infection, particularly reported in type 3 (10). In Shoji et al, 80% of neonates and infants with HPeV type 3 infection showed palmar and plantar rash, 58% with inclusion of trunk and limbs (12).HPeV type 3 is known to cause especially severe symptoms in young infants. A study of Hara et al. suggests these sepsis-like symptoms may be caused by an haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)-like disease due to an aberrant immune response. HLH is a severe hyperinflammatory syndrome due to immune dysregulation marked by elevated ferritin and cytopenia. Hyperferritinaemia and cytopenia are described to indicate hypercytokinemia. Hara et al. demonstrated elevated ferritin levels in infants with HPeV type 3 infection on day four to five in comparison to patients with enterovirus infection. Ferritin concentrations were higher in infants with apnea than in those without (13). Although the precise mechanisms underlying the particularly severe manifestations of HPeV type 3 infection in young infants remain unclear, these findings suggest that an HLH-like immune response may contribute to disease severity in this age group.On the other hand, another case series regarding neonates and infants with sepsis and HLH-like illness in HPeV type 3 infection showed elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST), soluble interleukin-2 receptor and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) in all cases (14).AST and LDH were normal in our patient while we did not measure ferritin and the soluble interleukin 2 receptor. This suggests that in cases of severe presentation of HPeV infection, laboratory measurements should include indicators of HLH-like illness. The specific genotype would have been of interest in this case as well, in order to help clarify the cause of this particularly severe course. As described above, the patient's rash and sepsis-like presentation in combination with encephalitis might indicate an infection with HPeV type 3.Apart from leukopenia, the patient exhibited no clinically significant laboratory abnormalities. This paucity of laboratory findings is consistent with previous reports. CSF pleocytosis is absent in most cases of HPeV infection, whereas leukopenia is a commonly reported finding (6, 7, 9, 15).At our institution, PCR testing for HPeV is not currently available for serum samples. More widespread availability of blood-based HPeV PCR testing could facilitate earlier diagnosis and potentially allow earlier discontinuation of empirical antibiotic treatment in young infants. As in our case, an important differential diagnosis is bacterial meningo-/ encephalitis which is why antibiotic treatment (ceftriaxone) was administered until receiving positive CSF PCR for HPeV and negative PCR for bacterial pathogens such as pneumococcus, meningococcus and haemophilus influenzae. In the present case, ceftriaxone was selected as the first-line empirical antibiotic until receiving these findings despite the accompanying gastrointestinal symptoms, as the clinical presentation raised concern for meningoencephalitis. This management was in accordance with our institution's treatment protocol.At our institution, HPeV is not included in the routine multiplex viral stool PCR panel; consequently, the stool sample could not be tested for HPeV. Expanding the range of pathogens included in such panels may improve the detection rate of viral infections in young infants.The literature supports collecting respiratory tract, stool, blood, and CSF samples for PCR testing to facilitate the early detection of viral pathogens, particularly HPeV (7). Broader access to appropriate molecular diagnostic testing may therefore improve the timely diagnosis of HPeV infection (7, 9).The diagnosis of HPeV encephalitis was primarily established by detection of viral RNA in the CSF using PCR. However, the assay used in this case did not determine the specific HPeV genotype.Overall, brain MRI is the imaging modality of choice for detecting white-matter abnormalities in patients with HPeV encephalitis. The extensive diffusion restriction observed on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) in our patient represents a characteristic neuroimaging pattern of HPeV encephalitis (7).Herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis represents an important differential diagnosis in neonates presenting with a sepsis-like clinical picture and focal seizures. Empirical treatment with aciclovir was therefore initiated in the present case. Neuroimaging can assist in distinguishing these conditions: HPeV encephalitis typically produces extensive, bilateral symmetrical white-matter diffusion restriction, whereas HSV encephalitis more commonly involves cortical and temporal regions. The predominantly white-matter pattern observed in our patient was therefore consistent with HPeV encephalitis (6, 15).Given the potentially severe consequences of untreated bacterial meningitis and herpes simplex virus encephalitis, empirical antibacterial and antiviral treatment was initiated immediately. This approach is consistent with recommendations to commence empirical anti-infective therapy in infants with suspected meningoencephalitis and to discontinue treatment once HPeV infection has been confirmed and bacterial and HSV infection have been excluded (4).Until the positive PCR result was received, the patient was given pyridoxine due to the differential diagnosis of vitamin B6-dependent epilepsy, which is rare but significant at this age. Neonates with this diagnosis show treatment-resistant seizures with various semiologies abnormal aEEG findings, such as a burst-suppression pattern. In vitamin B6-dependent epilepsy, early metabolic testing and treatment with pyridoxine are essential (16, 17).Other differential diagnoses of neonatal seizures include hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy, intracranial haemorrhage, cerebral infarction, disturbances of glucose or electrolyte homeostasis, congenital metabolic disorders, genetic epilepsies, haemodynamically significant congenital heart disease, and intoxication (18). The clinical examination, laboratory findings, microbiological results, echocardiography and neuroimaging did not provide evidence of the alternative diagnoses.As no specific antiviral therapy is currently available for HPeV infection, management is primarily supportive and directed towards acute complications. In addition, the greater permeability of the blood–brain barrier in young infants may facilitate viral neuroinvasion (7, 9, 10).Enteroviruses belong to the same viral family as HPeV and may cause a similar spectrum of disease, including fever, respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms, sepsis-like illness, (meningo-) encephalitis, hand, foot and mouth disease, herpangina, rash, myocarditis and hepatitis (11).Especially the generalized erythematous rash which our patient exhibited is a typical sign of HPeV infection, particularly reported in type 3 (10). In Shoji et al, 80% of neonates and infants with HPeV type 3 infection showed palmar and plantar rash, 58% with inclusion of trunk and limbs (12).HPeV type 3 is known to cause especially severe symptoms in young infants. A study of Hara et al. suggests these sepsis-like symptoms may be caused by an haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)-like disease due to an aberrant immune response. HLH is a severe hyperinflammatory syndrome due to immune dysregulation marked by elevated ferritin and cytopenia. Hyperferritinaemia and cytopenia are described to indicate hypercytokinemia. Hara et al. demonstrated elevated ferritin levels in infants with HPeV type 3 infection on day four to five in comparison to patients with enterovirus infection. Ferritin concentrations were higher in infants with apnea than in those without (13). Although the precise mechanisms underlying the particularly severe manifestations of HPeV type 3 infection in young infants remain unclear, these findings suggest that an HLH-like immune response may contribute to disease severity in this age group.On the other hand, another case series regarding neonates and infants with sepsis and HLH-like illness in HPeV type 3 infection showed elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST), soluble interleukin-2 receptor and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) in all cases (14).AST and LDH were normal in our patient while we did not measure ferritin and the soluble interleukin 2 receptor. This suggests that in cases of severe presentation of HPeV infection, laboratory measurements should include indicators of HLH-like illness. The specific genotype would have been of interest in this case as well, in order to help clarify the cause of this particularly severe course. As described above, the patient's rash and sepsis-like presentation in combination with encephalitis might indicate an infection with HPeV type 3.Apart from leukopenia, the patient exhibited no clinically significant laboratory abnormalities. This paucity of laboratory findings is consistent with previous reports. CSF pleocytosis is absent in most cases of HPeV infection, whereas leukopenia is a commonly reported finding (6, 7, 9, 15).At our institution, PCR testing for HPeV is not currently available for serum samples. More widespread availability of blood-based HPeV PCR testing could facilitate earlier diagnosis and potentially allow earlier discontinuation of empirical antibiotic treatment in young infants. As in our case, an important differential diagnosis is bacterial meningo-/ encephalitis which is why antibiotic treatment (ceftriaxone) was administered until receiving positive CSF PCR for HPeV and negative PCR for bacterial pathogens such as pneumococcus, meningococcus and haemophilus influenzae. In the present case, ceftriaxone was selected as the first-line empirical antibiotic until receiving these findings despite the accompanying gastrointestinal symptoms, as the clinical presentation raised concern for meningoencephalitis. This management was in accordance with our institution's treatment protocol.At our institution, HPeV is not included in the routine multiplex viral stool PCR panel; consequently, the stool sample could not be tested for HPeV. Expanding the range of pathogens included in such panels may improve the detection rate of viral infections in young infants.The literature supports collecting respiratory tract, stool, blood, and CSF samples for PCR testing to facilitate the early detection of viral pathogens, particularly HPeV (7). Broader access to appropriate molecular diagnostic testing may therefore improve the timely diagnosis of HPeV infection (7, 9).The diagnosis of HPeV encephalitis was primarily established by detection of viral RNA in the CSF using PCR. However, the assay used in this case did not determine the specific HPeV genotype.Overall, brain MRI is the imaging modality of choice for detecting white-matter abnormalities in patients with HPeV encephalitis. The extensive diffusion restriction observed on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) in our patient represents a characteristic neuroimaging pattern of HPeV encephalitis (7).Herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis represents an important differential diagnosis in neonates presenting with a sepsis-like clinical picture and focal seizures. Empirical treatment with aciclovir was therefore initiated in the present case. Neuroimaging can assist in distinguishing these conditions: HPeV encephalitis typically produces extensive, bilateral symmetrical white-matter diffusion restriction, whereas HSV encephalitis more commonly involves cortical and temporal regions. The predominantly white-matter pattern observed in our patient was therefore consistent with HPeV encephalitis (6, 15).Given the potentially severe consequences of untreated bacterial meningitis and herpes simplex virus encephalitis, empirical antibacterial and antiviral treatment was initiated immediately. This approach is consistent with recommendations to commence empirical anti-infective therapy in infants with suspected meningoencephalitis and to discontinue treatment once HPeV infection has been confirmed and bacterial and HSV infection have been excluded (4).Until the positive PCR result was received, the patient was given pyridoxine due to the differential diagnosis of vitamin B6-dependent epilepsy, which is rare but significant at this age. Neonates with this diagnosis show treatment-resistant seizures with various semiologies abnormal aEEG findings, such as a burst-suppression pattern. In vitamin B6-dependent epilepsy, early metabolic testing and treatment with pyridoxine are essential (16, 17).Other differential diagnoses of neonatal seizures include hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy, intracranial haemorrhage, cerebral infarction, disturbances of glucose or electrolyte homeostasis, congenital metabolic disorders, genetic epilepsies, haemodynamically significant congenital heart disease, and intoxication (18). full_text_sections.other: IntroductionHuman parechovirus (HPeV) is a common pathogen belonging to the family of picornaviridae, which also includes other virus types such as enterovirus or poliovirus and is associated especially with respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms. In most cases, infection is mild, and the majority of children have been infected by the age of three years (1). Among young infants presenting with fever without an identifiable source upon initial clinical assessment, HPeV is later detected in 6%–15% of cases (2, 3). Several studies have reported a male predominance, with male infants accounting for 56%–91% of cases (4).Among the 19 recognised HPeV genotypes, types 1 and 3 in particular have been associated with more severe disease (5). HPeV type 3 is the genotype predominantly involved in severe infections, especially among infants younger than three months. Whereas the clinical spectrum of parechovirus infection ranges from asymptomatic infection to rare cases of encephalitis, severe manifestations occur predominantly in this age group (4–7). Fever is the most common clinical manifestation, occurring in 80%–100% of reported cases. Erythema is reported in 20%–60% of cases, whereas seizures occur in 3%–65%. Other manifestations include diarrhea, respiratory symptoms, irritability, poor feeding and tachycardia (4).Laboratory abnormalities are generally mild and non-specific, with leukopenia being particularly common in infants younger than three months. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings are usually unremarkable, and pleocytosis is typically absent. Cranial ultrasonography is generally normal. In patients with neurological involvement, MRI is the imaging modality of choice and may reveal characteristic white-matter abnormalities (4).In a British study by Braccio et al., 83% of patients with HPeV infection admitted to a paediatric intensive care unit (PICU) were younger than one year, and 40% presented with neurological manifestations. Neurological complications were particularly common among infants younger than three months, occurring in 46% of this age group. Invasive mechanical ventilation was required in 77% of patients admitted to the PICU. The mortality rate was approximately 8% (8). In other studies among infants with severe neurological manifestations of HPeV type 3 infection, reported mortality rates range from 1.6% to 6% (5).Here, we report an exceptionally severe case of HPeV infection in a young infant. Case descriptionMedical historyA two-week-old male infant presented to our emergency department with fever. His stools had been slightly looser than usual; however, oral intake remained adequate. Several family members were experiencing symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection at the time of presentation. He had been born by uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery at 37 + 2 weeks of gestation, with a birth weight of 3,300 g. Maternal group B streptococcus colonisation status was unknown. The infant had otherwise been healthy and was receiving routine vitamin D supplementation.Clinical findingsOn admission, the infant was in an age-appropriate nutritional state but appeared generally unwell. His skin was pale pink, with mottling of the limbs. The anterior fontanelle was soft and flat. Heart sounds were normal and regular. Respiratory, abdominal, and ear, nose, and throat examinations were unremarkable.On neurological examination, the infant was somnolent but arousable and exhibited a high-pitched cry. Spontaneous movements, muscle tone, and strength were symmetrical.Because of the fever, the patient was initially admitted to the general paediatric ward for clinical observation. During the first hours of his inpatient stay, he developed recurrent apnoeas and seizures and was therefore transferred to the PICU.Following transfer to the PICU, the recurrent seizures were characterised more precisely as predominantly unilateral twitching of the upper limbs, occasionally accompanied by lip smacking. Individual episodes lasted 10–30 s and were associated with apnea and oxygen desaturation.During hospital stay, the infant developed a generalised erythematous rash. papers.title: Longitudinal Surface Water Viral Surveillance Following the 2024 Extreme Flood: One-Year Monitoring in Porto Alegre, Brazil.
papers.abstract: Abstract Extreme flood events can overwhelm sanitation infrastructure and drive the widespread dispersal of viral pathogens into aquatic environments. In May 2024, Porto Alegre (southern Brazil) experienced an unprecedented flood that caused record-breaking overflow of the Guaíba hydrological system and prolonged urban inundation. Here we report a one-year longitudinal environmental viral surveillance study, comprising seven campaigns between May 2024 and April 2025. Surface waters were analyzed by RT-qPCR for SARS-CoV-2, norovirus genogroups I and II, hepatitis A virus (HAV) and hepatitis E virus (HEV). papers.title: EpiLinx - An interactive tool for establishing epidemiological links as part of national nosocomial outbreak investigation.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Healthcare-associated infections remain a major public health challenge worldwide. Effective surveillance requires timely identification of epidemiological links. Although electronic health records are widely used, their complexity often hinder rapid analysis in practice. We developed EpiLinx, a user-friendly tool that uses administrative patient data to support systematic investigation of suspected outbreaks in healthcare settings. The aim of this paper is to present EpiLinx and assess its usability against two real-life healthcare associated outbreaks. METHODS: EpiLinx is an R shiny application that identifies spatio-temporal overlaps between patients' hospital contacts in extensive datasets. It provides interactive tables and visualizations, including timelines and network diagrams, to support rapid data exploration. The software is designed to be generic with minimal data requirements to ensure accessibility for non-technical users. RESULTS: EpiLinx was applied to a Danish Enterobacter hormaechei outbreak and a British norovirus outbreak. In both cases, EpiLinx rapidly generated visualizations and network structures consistent with the conclusions of the original investigations. Analyses that previously required hours of manual data handling were completed within seconds. CONCLUSION: EpiLinx enables rapid and intuitive exploration of epidemiological links in large healthcare datasets, supporting more timely outbreak investigations. Its simplicity and minimal data requirements make it readily applicable in clinical practice, including for non-technical users. The approach is broadly applicable across settings where routinely collected administrative data are available. By improving transparency and accessibility in link assessment, EpiLinx has the potential to strengthen infection control in both clinical and public health contexts.

papers.abstract_zh: 背景:医疗保健相关感染仍然是全球主要的公共卫生挑战。有效的监测需要及时识别流行病学联系。尽管电子健康记录被广泛使用,但其复杂性往往阻碍了实践中的快速分析。我们开发了 EpiLinx,这是一种用户友好的工具,它使用管理患者数据来支持医疗机构中可疑 暴发 的系统调查。本文的目的是介绍 EpiLinx 并评估其针对两个现实生活中的医疗保健相关 暴发 的可用性。方法:EpiLinx 是一款 R 闪亮应用程序,可识别大量数据集中患者医院联系人之间的时空重叠。它提供交互式表格和可视化,包括时间线和网络图,以支持快速数据探索。该软件设计为通用型,具有最少的数据要求,以确保非技术用户的可访问性。结果:EpiLinx 应用于丹麦霍马氏肠杆菌 暴发 和英国 诺如病毒 暴发。在这两种情况下,EpiLinx 都快速生成了与原始调查结论一致的可视化和网络结构。以前需要数小时的手动数据处理的分析在几秒钟内完成。结论:EpiLinx 能够快速、直观地探索大型医疗数据集中的流行病学联系,支持更及时的 暴发 调查。其简单性和最少的数据要求使其易于应用于临床实践,包括非技术用户。该方法广泛适用于可以获得常规收集的管理数据的环境。通过提高关联评估的透明度和可访问性,EpiLinx 有潜力加强临床和公共卫生环境中的感染控制。

papers.title: Climate Change, Waterborne Pathogens, and the Future of WASH
papers.abstract: Climate change is altering hydrological cycles, water temperature, precipitation extremes, drought frequency, and infrastructure reliability, reshaping exposure to waterborne pathogens. This chapter examines how these changes affect bacteria, viruses, and protozoa, including Vibrio cholerae, pathogenic Escherichia coli, Salmonella, Campylobacter, norovirus, rotavirus, Cryptosporidium, and Giardia, and how failures across water, sanitation, and hygiene systems amplify risk. It integrates climate-resilient water and sanitation safety planning with digital microbiology, including online sensors, remote sensing, molecular diagnostics, metagenomics, wastewater surveillance, quantitative microbial risk assessment, and AI-based early warning. The future of WASH will depend on resilient infrastructure, inclusive governance, continuous microbial surveillance, locally calibrated predictive models, and rapid translation of environmental signals into preventive action.

papers.title: Caracterització de virus entèrics en aigües residuals i regenerades
papers.abstract: [ES] Los virus son patógenos relevantes para la salud pública, con capacidad de provocar enfermedades agudas, crónicas e incluso letales. Los alimentos y el agua suponen dos de las fuentes de transmisión de virus más importantes, principalmente de virus transmitidos a través de la ruta fecal-oral, conocidos como virus entéricos. En el contexto del ciclo hidrológico urbano, las aguas residuales domésticas pueden contener virus excretados en heces, que, cuando no se utilizan los procesos de regeneración de agua residual correctos, pueden llegar a los efluentes de las estaciones de tratamiento de agua residual (EDAR). La reutilización de estas aguas regeneradas contaminadas para riego agrícola o usos industriales plantea riesgos potenciales de diseminación vírica. Es por ello que la vigilancia virológica en aguas regeneradas es esencial para evaluar la eficacia de los procesos de depuración y mitigar el riesgo de transmisión viral a través de la cadena alimentaria o el ambiente, especialmente cuando dicho agua se destina al riego de cultivos o procesos industriales susceptibles de contaminación biológica. El objetivo de este estudio se centra en comparar la presencia y diversidad de virus entéricos (norovirus humanos, virus de las hepatitis A y E, rotavirus y enterovirus) en las aguas de entrada y salida de cuatro estaciones depuradoras, antes y después de diferentes tratamientos de regeneración, mediante técnicas de biología molecular (qPCR) y secuenciación masiva. Esto permitirá tanto conocer las concentraciones virales en los influentes y los genotipos circulantes como la capacidad de las EDAR para la eliminación de virus.

papers.abstract_zh: [ES] 病毒与公共健康有关,具有挑衅性、历史性和包括性的能力。食物和水的供应是病毒传播的重要因素,病毒通过粪便-口腔传播的原理,是肠道病毒的传播途径。在城市水环境背景下,国内水残留物中含有病毒排泄物,因此,我们无法利用残留水校正再生过程,将水残留物和水残留物排放物 (EDAR) 排出。重新利用农业或工业植物中污染的水,以消除病毒传播的潜力。病毒预防和水再生是对净化过程的功效和减轻病毒传播以及食品和环境中的病毒传播进行重要评估,特别是对栽培过程的目的而言工业易受生物污染。该研究的目的是比较肠道病毒的存在和多样性(诺如病毒 人类、甲型肝炎病毒和戊型肝炎病毒、轮状病毒和肠道病毒)以及四肢的水和唾液,以及不同病原体的前奏和设计再生、分子生物学中间技术 (qPCR) 和维护。允许病毒浓度与 EDAR 的影响力和基因循环能力一起消除病毒。

MIRROR+ Mirror+ Exclusives Mirror+ Rewards Mirror+ Newsletters Celebs TV Emmerdale Coronation Street Films Hollywood Pride of Britain I'm A Celebrity Partner Stories Horoscopes Online Games Crossword Solitaire Sudoku Mahjong Bingo Sport Football Boxing UFC Cricket Rugby Union Rugby League F1 Racing Golf Athletics Darts Snooker US Sports Betting Lifestyle Family Health Sex & Relationships Money Gardening Shopping Fashion & Beauty Food & Drink Motoring Tech Gaming Travel UK & Ireland Europe USA & Canada Caribbean Africa Cruises Cheap Flights Asia & Middle East Australia & New Zealand Central & South America InYourArea Funeral Notices Shop Competitions Offers Newsletter Signup Follow us on social News World news Norovirus Düsseldorf Airport mass casualty response after 'norovirus outbreak' on flight Düsseldorf Airport reportedly activated its mass casualty response after several passengers fell ill during a Eurowings flight Add to preferred sources Comments5 News Eliana Nunes News Reporter 10:28, 21 Oct 2026Updated 17:03, 23 Oct 2026 Powered By 10 Sec Suspected Norovirus outbreak on Eurowings flight from Greece to Germany Next Stay Suspected Norovirus outbreak on Eurowings flight from Greece to Germany Several passengers on board a Eurowings flight fell ill with suspected norovirus amid an outbreak on the Greek island of Rhodes. Article continues below Passengers began experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms during flight EW9631 from Rhodes to Düsseldorf, Germany, on Sunday evening. The cabin crew requested a priority landing at Düsseldorf Airport, a Eurowings spokesperson said. ‌ The airport activated its mass casualty response, according to German news site aero.de, with medics in "hazmat suits" boarding the plane as soon as it landed. Three passengers were taken to hospital. Article continues below The illnesses are believed to be linked to a norovirus outbreak on Rhodes that has been ongoing since July. Norovirus, commonly known as the winter vomiting bug, causes vomiting and diarrhoea, the NHS says. View 3 Images Medics pictured on board flight EW9631 after it landed in Germany(Image: Jam Press/@naeddaspin) ‌ READ MORE: Met Office issues amber warning for Storm Austen – 4 areas face ‘danger to life’ READ MORE: 'Cold-blooded' student stabbed housemate 30 times to death after lying in wait in their garden Greek newspaper Kathimerini reported on October 2 that more than 1,400 patients with gastrointestinal symptoms linked to the outbreak had been treated at Rhodes Hospital since August 10. At the time, the newspaper said the total number of cases recorded since mid-July was close to 1,800. However, it added that the actual figure was likely to be higher, as the total did not include patients treated by private doctors or those who had not sought hospital treatment. Article continues below Nathalie Gombik, 28, was travelling back home to Germany with her partner after a holiday when the incident unfolded. "Seeing so many ambulances and emergency personnel in protective clothing after landing was quite shocking," she said. Article continues below View 3 Images Nathalie Gombik and her partner Caz(Image: Jam Press/@naeddaspin) "During the flight, several passengers became ill. I know for certain that three passengers were affected, but it appeared that approximately three more were also experiencing symptoms. Some passengers were vomiting during the flight." Article continues below Nathalie praised the German airline's cabin crew for remaining "calm" and "discreet" throughout the flight. "At the time, we had no idea that a mass casualty incident had reportedly been declared, that numerous ambulances had been mobilised or that our aircraft had reportedly been given priority for landing," she added. Article continues below She said passengers had to remain on board for around 90 minutes before they were allowed to disembark. Nathalie added that she began experiencing similar symptoms on Tuesday, two days after the flight. Article continues below View 3 Images A Eurowings spokesperson said several guests 'felt very unwell' during flight EW9631(Image: Jam Press/@naeddaspin) A Eurowings spokesperson said: "We can confirm that several guests on Eurowings flight EW9631 from Rhodes to Dusseldorf on 18 October 2026 felt very unwell during the flight. Article continues below "The flight crew therefore requested a priority landing at Dusseldorf Airport. After landing, medical staff examined and cared for three affected guests on site. As a precaution, these guests went to hospital. All other guests continued their journeys home as normal. "There were 212 guests and seven crew members on board. The cause of the symptoms is unclear and is being looked into. The safety and health of our guests and crews is always Eurowings' top priority." Article continues below The NHS says norovirus spreads through close contact with infected people, contaminated surfaces, infected food or water, and food prepared by someone carrying the virus. Although unpleasant, symptoms usually improve within about two days. GET MORE FROM US Choose Daily Mirror as a 'Preferred Source' on Google News for quick access to the news you value. news.content_zh: 2026 年 10 月 23 日,从罗德岛飞往德国杜塞尔多夫的欧洲之翼航班上的几名乘客疑似感染 诺如病毒,促使杜塞尔多夫机场启动了大规模伤亡应对措施。三名乘客被送往医院。罗德岛的 诺如病毒 暴发 自 7 月以来一直在进行,已报告了 1,400 多例病例。欧洲之翼证实,几名乘客在飞行过程中感到不适,身着防护服的医务人员登上飞机检查和照顾受影响的乘客。

Clipart Korea** Norovirus has been detected in connection with an outbreak at an elementary school in Suncheon, South Jeolla Province, where 228 students reported symptoms of suspected food poisoning. Authorities have yet to confirm whether the virus entered through school meals or drinking water. 228 Students Affected as Norovirus Confirmed The Suncheon Public Health Center said on the 27th that tests by the Jeonnam Institute of Health and Environment on human specimens from students suspected of infection confirmed the presence of norovirus. Norovirus is a collective term for a group of viruses divided into several types based on genetic characteristics. The incubation period after infection is typically 12 to 48 hours, with vomiting, diarrhea and abdominal pain appearing abruptly and lasting one to three days. Healthy adults generally recover with adequate fluid intake, but children and older adults require closer attention because dehydration can progress rapidly. Hygiene management is also important because the virus can still spread after symptoms disappear. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says the virus can be detected in stool for two weeks or more after recovery and recommends following preventive measures such as handwashing. Students at the school began showing suspected food poisoning symptoms including vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhea starting on the 17th. A full survey identified 228 students with symptoms. Jeonnam-Gwangju Special Metropolitan City, the city of Suncheon and the Suncheon Office of Education collected specimens from students and requested analysis to determine the cause. Were School Meals the Source? Investigation Into Transmission Route Continues Test results for school meals, facilities and drinking water have not yet been reported, leaving the route of transmission unconfirmed. Authorities are examining whether meals served on the 16th were linked to the infections and plan to take follow-up steps once the analysis is complete. If management problems are found in the group meal service, corresponding measures will be taken. A similar case of suspected mass food poisoning at a school occurred earlier in Gongju, South Chungcheong Province. On June 16, students and teachers at an elementary school in Gongju showed similar symptoms, prompting health authorities to launch an emergency epidemiological investigation. At the school, which has about 980 students enrolled, the number of symptomatic cases rose to 365. The school ran shortened morning classes through the 22nd of the same month and provided substitute meals instead of regular school lunches. Temporary closure was also considered at the time given the possibility of further spread. Healthy Living Overland Park Elementary Norovirus Outbreak Ends After 97 Illnesses as Johnson County Warns the True Count Is Higher Published Oct 22, 2026 10:55 PM EDT By Dorothy Brooks OLI SCARFF | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on WhatsApp Johnson County health officials have declared a norovirus outbreak at Bentwood Elementary School in south Overland Park after 97 people fell ill, KCTV5 reported on October 21. Of those, 95 cases were among students and staff inside the school, and two were among family members outside it, Johnson County Department of Health and Environment Director Charlie Hunt said. Hunt said the true number is likely higher because norovirus is so contagious. Mild cases often go unreported, and some families likely cared for sick children at home without contacting anyone. The school sits near 129th Street and Quivira Road but belongs to the Olathe School District. For Kansas City-area parents, the episode is an early reminder that stomach bugs spread fast in classrooms, even as flu cases begin to rise. Inside the Bentwood Timeline The district said absences involving similar symptoms first appeared on Thursday, October 8. Students were out the next day for a scheduled professional development day, and crews deep-cleaned the building that weekend. On Monday, October 12, absences reached 10%, the threshold that triggers contact with the Johnson County Department of Health and Environment. The department then began determining whether the illnesses met the definition of an outbreak, while custodians deep-cleaned and disinfected high-touch surfaces and high-traffic areas daily. The building was cleaned again during scheduled days off later that week. Two people with symptoms tested positive for norovirus. Based on those results and 82 other people who reported similar symptoms between October 8 and 14, the county declared an outbreak. Health officials said the cases were epidemiologically linked, meaning people had similar symptoms at the same time in the same setting. The total later grew to 97. The county and district notified Bentwood families on October 19. Parent Samantha Pedraza said she first heard about the outbreak through parent text messages and apps before that notice arrived, and she knows of families where several children or parents got sick. "I was surprised we had such a heavy amount of it so quickly," she said. By Wednesday, October 21, only one student was absent with similar symptoms, according to the district. Officials have not publicly identified a source. Norovirus outbreaks in schools often spread from person to person and through contaminated surfaces, which can make a single starting point hard to pin down. Why the Virus Moves So Fast Through Classrooms Norovirus infects the digestive tract and causes nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. According to the CDC, it spreads through direct contact with sick people, contaminated food or water and contaminated surfaces. Dr. Dana Hawkinson, medical director of infection prevention and control at the University of Kansas Health System, said the virus easily contaminates shared spaces, and its tiny particles make it hard to know when you have touched them. His advice for families was direct: "Do adequate hand washing, especially after using the restroom." Hawkinson stressed soap and water, and Pedraza said she has emphasized handwashing with her child because hand sanitizer does not work well against norovirus. She said the school nurse posted handwashing signs for students. Disinfecting doorknobs, counters, and phones also helps. Hawkinson said sick children should stay home for at least 48 hours and until they are better and can control their bowel movements. Sick adults should stay home from work for the same reason. Hunt noted there is no vaccine for norovirus, and antibiotics do not work against it because it is a virus. Johnson County typically sees three to five norovirus outbreaks a year, ranging from a handful of cases to a couple dozen, he said. Bentwood was on the larger side, but not record-setting. Nationally, about 2,500 norovirus outbreaks are reported each year, according to the CDC's outbreak data, a figure Hunt said is also likely an undercount. Families Most at Risk and When to Seek Care Most people recover in two to three days without specific treatment. The main danger is dehydration from fluid loss, which hits hardest in the very young, older adults and people with weakened immune systems or chronic illness, Hawkinson said. Warning signs of dehydration include urinating very little, a dry mouth, and dizziness when standing. In young children, crying with few or no tears and unusual sleepiness are also red flags. Parents should call a pediatrician if a child cannot keep fluids down and seek urgent care for signs of severe dehydration or a child who is hard to wake. Immunity after infection fades. Hawkinson said people likely have some protection for the next two to three weeks but can be infected again months later, so a household that already had the virus should not drop its guard for the whole season. For working parents, the practical cost is missed school and work. Keeping a child home for the full 48 hours can be hard, but sending children back early helps the virus keep spreading. MedicalDaily will watch for new school or child-care clusters in Johnson County as winter approaches. The Bentwood outbreak is over, but steady handwashing remains a household's strongest defense. Johnson County confirmed a norovirus outbreak that sickened 97 people, including 95 students and staff, and has since declared it over. Was the source found? Officials have not publicly identified a source. The illnesses were linked by timing, setting, and symptoms, with two lab-confirmed cases. What are the symptoms of norovirus? Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, which usually last two to three days. Does hand sanitizer stop norovirus? Not reliably. Washing hands with soap and water and disinfecting high-touch surfaces work better. When can a sick child return to school? A University of Kansas Health System expert advised waiting at least 48 hours and until the child has recovered. Who should seek medical care? Anyone showing signs of dehydration, especially young children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems.
